mainTopic: When a woman may blame a blood stain (כתם) on an outside source and stay טהורה
overview: The amud opens by finishing the case of רב ששת. The גמרא explains that the case of two women and one bird is different, because the bird could explain only one סלע of blood. A ברייתא then teaches that a stain on layered robes can be blamed on an outside source only if one really exists, like the butchers' market. A new משנה lists things a woman may blame a stain on: slaughtering, handling stains, a louse, or a wound that could reopen. It also tells how רבי עקיבא ruled leniently, explaining that by Torah law only 'דם' makes her טמאה, not a stain. The גמרא reads the משנה closely: she may blame a source only if she was surely exposed to it. On the louse, it brings the argument between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the חכמים, which is settled by the split-bean limit of רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס, and it describes the bedbug and a town with pigs. Finally רב הונא and רב חסדא argue whether a stain exactly the size of a גריס may be blamed, and a challenge begins that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why is this different from the two women and one bird?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the earlier ruling of רב ששת from a ברייתא where two women handled one bird and both are טמאות.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is this different from the ברייתא: two women handled one bird that only had enough blood for one סלע-sized stain, and a סלע-sized stain was found on each of them, and both are טמאות?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to clash with the ruling in רב ששת's case, which was just discussed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the bird case, one woman's stain could have come from the bird, yet both women are טמאות. That suggests we should be strict on everyone, so why was one woman left טהורה in רב ששת's case?

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference? A challenge from a case that seems similar
Bird; here, one that was slaughtered
A coin; used as a size measure for a stain

phrases.english: What is different from that which was taught in a ברייתא:
phrases.notes: "This" is רב ששת's case from just before, where one woman was left טהורה.

phrases.english: Two women who were busy with one bird,
and it has only a סלע's worth of blood,
and a סלע-sized stain was found on this one
and a סלע-sized stain on that one —
both of them are impure?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling in רב ששת's case from the end of the earlier discussion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in רב ששת's case that one of the women stays טהורה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the bird case, even though one stain could be blamed on the bird, both women are טמאות. So in רב ששת's case the second woman should also be טמאה.

steps.title: In the bird case there is an extra סלע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the bird case is different because there is one סלע of blood too many.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it is different, because there is an extra סלע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by pointing to a key difference between the two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bird could only explain one סלע, but two were found. So one stain surely came from a woman, and since we can't tell which one, both are טמאות. In רב ששת's case there is no such extra stain that must come from a woman.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there; a standard way to split two cases apart
Extra, more than can be explained

steps.whatToRemember: We blame a stain on an outside source only if the outside source can explain all the blood. If there is extra blood that must have come from a woman, and we don't know which woman, both are טמאות.

phrases.english: There it is different,
because there is an extra סלע.
phrases.notes: The bird only had one סלע of blood, so the second stain had to come from one of the women.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The bird case seemed to show we must always be strict on both women.
steps.terutzMaskana: The bird case is strict only because one stain definitely came from a woman; without an extra stain, the ruling in רב ששת's case stands.

steps.title: Three checked robes: what matters is whether she can blame something
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that with three checked robes, the layer the stain is on doesn't decide. What decides is whether there is something to blame it on.
steps.simpleTranslation: If she wore three robes that she had checked: if she can blame the stain on something, she may, even if it is on the bottom robe. If she can't blame it on something, she may not, even if it is on the top robe.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא with a clear rule about stains found on layered clothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think a stain on the inner robe, touching her body, must be from her, and one on the outer robe must be from outside. The ברייתא says no: the only question is whether there is a real outside source she can blame.

keyTerms.meaning: Checked, already examined and known to be clean
To blame, to say the blood came from another source
The bottom or inner layer, closest to her skin

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the position of the stain decides. Even a stain on the outer robe makes her טמאה if there is nothing to blame it on.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If she wore three robes that she had checked,
if she can blame it on something, she may blame it,
even if it is on the bottom one.
If she can't blame it on something, she may not blame it,
even if it is on the top one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new ברייתא on the same subject of blaming stains on outside sources.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whether she may blame a stain on something else depends only on whether there is a real outside source, not on which robe the stain is on.

steps.title: Example: walking through the butchers' market
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives an example: if she walked through the butchers' market she may blame even a stain on the bottom robe; if not, not even one on the top robe.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? If she walked through the butchers' market, she may blame it even on the bottom robe. If she did not, she may not blame it even on the top robe.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains its rule with a real-life example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The butchers' market is full of blood, so she has a real source to blame. Without such a place, she has nothing to blame, so the stain counts as hers wherever it is.

keyTerms.meaning: The butchers' market, a place with lots of blood

steps.whatToRemember: A stain can be blamed on an outside source only when there really was one, like walking through the butchers' market.

phrases.english: How so? If she passed through the butchers' market —
she may blame it, even on the bottom robe;
if she did not pass through the butchers' market —
even on the top robe she may not blame it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the general rule of step 3 with an example.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Walking through the butchers' market counts as a real outside source; without it, there is nothing to blame.

steps.title: משנה: things a woman may blame a stain on
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that a woman may blame a stain on anything that could reasonably explain it, and lists examples.
steps.simpleTranslation: She may blame a stain on anything she reasonably can: if she slaughtered a domestic animal, a wild animal, or a bird; if she was busy with stains; if she sat next to people busy with them; or if she killed a louse. In all these cases she may blame it on that.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins and lists the kinds of things a woman may blame a blood stain on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This matches the ברייתא we just learned: any real outside source of blood is enough. The list includes big sources, like slaughtering, and very small ones, like killing a louse.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה; marks the start of a new משנה
A wild animal, like a deer, as opposed to a domestic בהמה
A louse; killing one leaves a small spot of blood

steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה sets the basic rule that runs through the next discussion: a stain is not treated as נדה blood if there is a real outside source to blame it on.

phrases.english: משנה: And she may blame it on anything
that she is able to blame it on.
If she slaughtered a domestic animal, a wild animal, or a bird,
if she was busy with blood stains,
or if she sat next to those busy with them,
if she killed a louse —
she may blame it on that.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי' וְתוֹלָה בְּכׇל דָּבָר שֶׁהִיא יְכוֹלָה לִתְלוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה that continues the same theme as the ברייתא of steps 3 and 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman may blame a stain on any real outside source of blood: slaughtering, handling stains, sitting near people handling stains, or killing a louse.

steps.title: How large a stain can be blamed?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks what the size limit is for blaming a stain on a louse.
steps.simpleTranslation: Up to what size may she blame a stain?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks a question to set up the next move: how big a stain can be and still be blamed on something else, like a louse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said she may blame a stain on things like a louse. Now the משנה asks for a limit, because a very large stain could not come from a small crushed bug.

keyTerms.meaning: Up to how much? (asking for a size limit)
She blames it (on another source), so she stays טהורה
A blood stain found on her body or clothes, not a direct flow

phrases.english: Up to how much may she attribute?
phrases.notes: He means blaming the stain on a louse, from the list in the משנה just before.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the size limit on the general rule of blaming given in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The maximum size of a stain that may be blamed on a louse.

steps.title: Up to the size of a split bean
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס says she may blame a stain up to the size of a split bean on a louse, even if she does not remember killing one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס says: up to the size of a split bean, and even if she did not kill a louse.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס answers the question. A stain up to the size of a split bean may be blamed on a louse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A crushed louse can leave a stain up to about that size, so anything that big or smaller can be explained this way. She does not need to remember killing a louse. It is enough that it could have happened.

keyTerms.meaning: The size of a split bean, a standard measure for stains

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus says:
Up to the size of a split bean,
and even if she did not kill it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the size question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Up to a split bean, even without remembering killing a louse.

steps.title: Blaming a stain on a wound
steps.stepSummary: She may blame a stain on her son or husband if they have a wound. She may also blame it on her own wound if it could reopen and bleed.
steps.simpleTranslation: She may blame it on her son or her husband. And if she has a wound that could reopen and bleed, she may blame it on that.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds more things she may blame a stain on: a wound on her son or husband, or a wound of her own that could still bleed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Blood from people close to her can easily land on her clothes. Even her own wound counts if it has scabbed over, as long as it could open again and bleed.

keyTerms.meaning: On her son or on her husband

phrases.english: And she may attribute it to her son or to her husband,
if she has a wound,
and it can reopen and bleed,
that woman may attribute it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more sources a stain may be blamed on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A stain may be blamed on a wound of her son or husband, or on her own wound that could reopen and bleed.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא purifies a woman with a healed wound
steps.stepSummary: A woman told רבי עקיבא she saw a stain and had a healed wound that could reopen. He declared her טהורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A woman came to רבי עקיבא and said she saw a stain. He asked if she had a wound. She said yes, and that it healed. He asked if it could reopen and bleed. She said yes, and he declared her טהורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה tells a story that shows the rule about her own wound being put into practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the wound had already healed, it could still reopen. That was enough for רבי עקיבא to blame the stain on it. This backs up the rule in step 8.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident, a story brought as an example

phrases.english: There was an incident with one woman
who came before Rabbi Akiva.
She said to him: I saw a stain.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהּ: שֶׁמָּא מַכָּה הָיְתָה בִּיךְ?
phrases.english: He said to her: Perhaps you had a wound?
She said to him: Yes, and it healed.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהּ: שֶׁמָּא יְכוֹלָה לְהִגָּלֵעַ וּלְהוֹצִיא דָּם?
phrases.english: He said to her: Perhaps it could reopen and bleed?
She said to him: Yes.
And Rabbi Akiva declared her pure.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאִשָּׁה אַחַת שֶׁבָּאת לִפְנֵי רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real case showing the wound rule of step 8.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that she may blame a stain on her own wound that could reopen.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי עקיבא's ruling in the story.

steps.title: The students are surprised
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא saw his students looking at each other in surprise and asked what bothered them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He saw his students looking at each other. He said: What about this is hard for you?
steps.whatsHappening: The students seem surprised by how lenient the ruling was. רבי עקיבא asks what bothers them, setting up his explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The students' unspoken question is: why be so lenient when the wound had already healed? Asking it out loud gives רבי עקיבא the chance to explain the reason behind all the תולה rules.

phrases.english: He saw his students looking at one another.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: מָה הַדָּבָר קָשֶׁה בְּעֵינֵיכֶם?
phrases.english: He said to them: Why is this matter difficult in your eyes?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises the students' surprise at the ruling in step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי עקיבא ruled so leniently.

steps.title: Stains were made טמא only to be applied leniently
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא explains that the Torah makes a woman טמאה through 'דם', not a stain. So the חכמים' rule about stains is meant to be applied leniently.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים did not make this rule to be strict but to be lenient, as it says: 'And a woman who has a flow, her flow in her flesh being blood'. Blood, and not a stain.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא gives the reason for his ruling. By Torah law a stain does not make her טמאה, so wherever the stain can be explained away, we are lenient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא reads the word 'דם' in the פסוק: the Torah makes her טמאה through blood, not through a stain. So the טומאה of a כתם is only מדרבנן, and the חכמים set it up with room for leniency, like blaming it on other sources.

keyTerms.meaning: Blood, and not a stain: only a real flow is טמא by Torah law

steps.whatToRemember: The טומאה of a כתם is only מדרבנן. That is why we may blame it on any reasonable source and rule leniently.
steps.whyThisMatters: This reason explains the whole system of תולה: because stains are only טמא מדרבנן, any reasonable explanation is enough to keep her טהורה.

phrases.english: For the Sages did not state the matter
to be stringent but to be lenient,
as it is stated: "And if a woman has a flow,
her flow in her flesh being blood" —
"blood," and not a stain.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁלֹּא אָמְרוּ חֲכָמִים הַדָּבָר לְהַחְמִיר אֶלָּא לְהָקֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the students' question from step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Stains are טמא only מדרבנן, as the פסוק says 'דם' and not 'כתם', so the rule is meant to be applied leniently.

steps.title: A checking cloth found with blood under the pillow
steps.stepSummary: If an עד placed under a pillow is found with blood, a round stain is טהור and a long, smeared stain is טמא, according to רבי אליעזר ברבי צדוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: A checking cloth placed under the pillow with blood found on it: if round, it is טהור; if long, it is טמא. These are the words of רבי אליעזר ברבי צדוק.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens a new case: a checking cloth was put under a pillow and later found with blood. We need to know whether the blood is from her body or from a crushed louse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A round stain looks like a crushed louse, so she is טהורה. A long, wiped stain looks like the mark left by checking herself, so she is טמאה. The shape of the stain decides what we blame it on.

keyTerms.meaning: A cloth used for checking herself

phrases.english: A checking cloth that was placed under the pillow,
and blood was found on it:
if round, it is pure; if elongated, it is impure.
These are the words of Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Tzadok.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case in the משנה about a checking cloth, still about deciding where blood came from.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blood on an עד under the pillow: round is טהור, long is טמא (רבי אליעזר ברבי צדוק).

steps.title: The משנה already teaches the ברייתא about the eye salve and the sycamore sap
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that the משנה's broad rule, that she may blame a stain on anything possible, already includes the ברייתא's cases where רבי מאיר blamed a stain on an eye salve and רבי blamed one on sycamore sap.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Our משנה already teaches what the רבנן taught in a ברייתא: there was a case where רבי מאיר blamed a stain on an eye salve, and רבי blamed a stain on the sap of a sycamore tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by connecting the משנה to a ברייתא. Real cases where great sages blamed stains on everyday things fit the משנה's rule that she may blame a stain on anything she can.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said she may be תולה on 'anything she can blame it on.' The ברייתא gives concrete examples: an eye salve and sycamore sap, both of which can leave red marks. These cases match the משנה, and they also show that this is not just theory. Leading sages actually ruled this way.

keyTerms.meaning: We already learned this: our משנה already teaches what the ברייתא says
He attributed or blamed (the stain on another cause)
An eye salve or eye ointment

phrases.english: GEMARA
We have learned in our mishna that which the Rabbis taught:
There was an incident, and Rabbi Meir attributed it to an eye salve,
and Rabbi attributed it to the sap of a sycamore.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא's explanation of the משנה's list of things she may blame a stain on.
steps.raayaObject: The משנה's general rule that she may blame a stain on anything possible
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא recording how רבי מאיר and רבי actually ruled

steps.title: Only if she definitely sat near the women cleaning bloodstains
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה's words 'or if she sat,' the גמרא learns that she may blame the stain only if she definitely sat next to women cleaning bloodstains.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says 'or if she sat.' If she sat there, yes, she may blame it. If she did not sit there, no, she may not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads a precise word in the משנה, 'sat,' and draws a lesson from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה could have said simply 'she was near them.' Saying 'she sat' means she must know for sure that she was right there with them. If she was only somewhere in the area, the stain cannot be blamed on them.

keyTerms.meaning: She sat (next to women who were cleaning bloodstains)

phrases.english: "Or if she sat."
phrases.notes: Quoting the משנה: she sat beside women who were cleaning bloodstains.

phrases.english: If she sat, yes, she may blame it;
if she did not sit, no, she may not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next line of the משנה and reads it closely.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: She may blame a stain on women cleaning bloodstains only if she definitely sat with them.

steps.title: The משנה matches the ברייתא about the butchers' market
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says that if she surely passed through the butchers' market, she may blame the stain on it even if it is unclear whether blood sprayed on her. If it is unclear whether she passed through at all, she is טמאה. This matches what the גמרא just learned from the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our משנה already teaches what the רבנן taught: if she passed through the butchers' market and it is unclear whether blood sprayed on her, she may blame the stain on it. If it is unclear whether she passed through at all, she is טמאה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the lesson it just learned from 'she sat' is the same rule a ברייתא states openly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two kinds of doubt here. If she knows she was exposed to the source and only doubts whether it reached her, she may blame it. If she doubts whether she was exposed at all, she may not blame it. This is the same rule as 'she sat, yes; did not sit, no.'
steps.confusionAlert: Both cases involve a doubt, yet the results are opposite. What matters is what the doubt is about: whether the blood reached her (she may blame it) or whether she was there at all (she may not).

phrases.english: We have learned in our mishna that which the Rabbis taught:
If she passed through a marketplace of butchers,

phrases.aramaic: סָפֵק נִיתַּז עָלֶיהָ סָפֵק לֹא נִיתַּז עָלֶיהָ — תּוֹלָה,
phrases.english: and it is uncertain whether blood sprayed on her or did not spray on her, she may attribute it;

phrases.aramaic: סָפֵק עָבְרָה סָפֵק לֹא עָבְרָה — טְמֵאָה.
phrases.english: if it is uncertain whether she passed by or did not pass by, she is impure.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנֵינָא לְהָא דְּתָנוּ רַבָּנַן: עָבְרָה בְּשׁוּק שֶׁל טַבָּחִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the lesson drawn from 'she sat' is the same rule a ברייתא states openly.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that she may blame a stain only on a source she was definitely exposed to
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about the butchers' market
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the general rule: she must be certain she was exposed to the source, though she need not be certain the blood reached her.

steps.title: Only if she definitely killed a louse
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה's words 'she killed a louse,' the גמרא learns that she may blame the stain on a louse only if she actually killed one.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says 'she killed a louse.' If she killed one, yes, she may blame it. If she did not kill one, no, she may not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the next line of the משנה the same careful way it read 'she sat.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Following the same pattern, the משנה seems to require that she actually killed a louse. If she did not, she cannot just assume a louse caused the stain. This reading sets up the next question.

phrases.english: "She killed a louse."
If she killed one, yes, she may blame it;
if she did not kill one, no, she may not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same close-reading pattern as step 14 on the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the משנה, she may blame a stain on a louse only if she actually killed one.

steps.title: Whose opinion is the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which תנא holds the view that she may blame a louse only if she killed one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view does the משנה follow?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks who the author of the משנה is. This question sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule just drawn from the משנה is debated. So the גמרא wants to find out which side the משנה follows.

phrases.english: Whose opinion is the mishna?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks who holds the rule the גמרא just drew from the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא holds that she may blame a louse only if she killed one

steps.title: It is רבן שמעון בן גמליאל; the חכמים are more lenient
steps.stepSummary: The משנה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who says she may blame a louse only if she killed one. The חכמים say she may blame a louse either way.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, as a ברייתא teaches: if she killed a louse, she may blame the stain on it; if she did not kill one, she may not. These are the words of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. The חכמים say: either way she may blame it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, and it quotes a ברייתא where the חכמים disagree with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל requires that she actually killed a louse, just like 'she sat' and the butchers' market. The חכמים are more lenient and let her blame a louse even if she did not kill one. This fits רבי עקיבא's idea that the rules about stains should be applied leniently.

keyTerms.meaning: She may attribute (the stain to that cause)
The Sages, here the majority view against רבן שמעון בן גמליאל

steps.whatToRemember: She may blame a stain only on a source she was surely exposed to (sitting with women cleaning stains, passing through the butchers' market). For a louse, the משנה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who requires that she killed one. The חכמים let her blame a louse even if she did not.

phrases.english: It is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,
as it is taught in a baraita: If she killed a louse, she may attribute the stain to it;
if she did not kill one, she may not attribute it;
these are the words of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
And the Rabbis say:
Either way, she may attribute it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל הִיא, דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 17's question by naming the author of the משנה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל; the חכמים disagree and allow blaming a louse even if she did not kill one.

steps.title: Both views have a problem
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that his own view leads to a problem with no limit, and his colleagues' view leads to a problem with no end.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said: according to my words there is no limit, and according to my colleagues' words there is no end.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל makes a short, puzzling statement that both his view and the חכמים's view cause a problem. This line sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 showed that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל lets her blame a louse only if she killed one, while the חכמים let her blame it either way. Here he admits that each view, taken alone, goes too far in one direction. The next two steps spell out each problem.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said:
According to my words, there is no limit,
phrases.notes: "My words" is his own rule from the last step: she may blame a louse only if she killed one.

phrases.english: and according to my colleagues' words, there is no end.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִדְבָרַי — אֵין קֵץ, וּלְדִבְרֵי חֲבֵרַי — אֵין סוֹף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל reflects on the problem with both sides of the disagreement quoted in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both the strict view and the lenient view about blaming a louse lead to extreme results.

steps.title: Problem with his own strict view
steps.stepSummary: If she may blame a stain on a louse only when she killed one, no woman would ever be pure for her husband, because every bed has some louse blood on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to my words there is no limit: there would be no woman who is pure for her husband, since there is no bed that does not have a few drops of louse blood on it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל explains the problem with his own view. If she may blame a louse only when she actually killed one, almost every woman would end up טמאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Louse blood is found on practically every bed. If a woman cannot blame those drops on lice unless she killed one, she would have to treat every tiny spot as נדה blood. That makes women permanently forbidden to their husbands, which cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: Pure for her husband (permitted to him)

phrases.english: According to my words, there is no limit:
for you would have no woman who is pure for her husband,
since you have no bed at all

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ כַּמָּה טִיפֵּי דַּם מַאֲכוֹלֶת.
phrases.english: that does not have several drops of louse blood on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִדְבָרַי אֵין קֵץ — שֶׁאֵין לְךָ אִשָּׁה שֶׁטְּהוֹרָה לְבַעְלָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first half of step 19, "no limit."
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The strict view would leave nearly every woman טמאה, because louse blood is on every bed.

steps.title: Problem with the lenient view
steps.stepSummary: If she may always blame a stain on a louse, no woman would ever be impure, because she could blame every drop on lice.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to my colleagues' words there is no end: there would be no woman who is not pure for her husband, since there is no sheet that does not have a few drops of blood on it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל now explains the problem with the חכמים's view. If she may always blame a louse, almost no woman would ever be טמאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the mirror image of the last step. Since every sheet has some drops of blood, a woman could always say "that came from a louse," even for real נדה blood. That makes the stain laws almost meaningless.

phrases.english: According to my colleagues' words, there is no end:

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין לְךָ אִשָּׁה שֶׁאֵינָהּ טְהוֹרָה לְבַעְלָהּ,
phrases.english: for you would have no woman who is not pure for her husband,
since you have no sheet at all
that does not have several drops of blood on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְדִבְרֵי חֲבֵרַי אֵין סוֹף — שֶׁאֵין לְךָ אִשָּׁה שֶׁאֵינָהּ טְהוֹרָה לְבַעְלָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second half of step 19, "no end."
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The lenient view would leave nearly every woman טהורה, because she could always blame a louse.

steps.title: Accepting the split-bean size limit
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל prefers the view of רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס: she may blame a stain on a louse up to the size of a split bean, and he agrees to this.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the words of רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס seem better than mine and theirs. He used to say: up to what size may she blame a stain? Up to the size of a split bean. And we agree with his words.
steps.whatsHappening: After showing the problem with both views, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל chooses a middle path. He accepts רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס's rule, which uses a size limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The middle path does not ask whether she killed a louse. It asks how big the stain is. A small stain, up to the size of a split bean, may be blamed on a louse, and a bigger one may not. This avoids both extremes from steps 20 and 21.

keyTerms.meaning: She blames (attributes) the stain on something else
The size of a split bean

steps.whatToRemember: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל ends up following רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס: a stain up to the size of a split bean may be blamed on a louse.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל נִרְאִין דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן אַנְטִיגְנוֹס
phrases.english: But the words of Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus seem better
than my words and their words,
for he used to say:
Up to what size may she blame a stain?
Up to the size of a split bean.
And we agree with his words.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל נִרְאִין דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן אַנְטִיגְנוֹס מִדְּבָרַי וּמִדִּבְרֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the problem raised in steps 19 to 21 by adopting a size-based middle position.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A stain up to the size of a split bean may be blamed on a louse. This is the view of רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל accepts it.
steps.whyThisMatters: It changes the test from "did she kill a louse?" to "how big is the stain?"

steps.title: What is the size limit for the רבנן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the רבנן allow her to blame a louse even without killing one, but up to what size may she do so?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the רבנן, who say she may blame a louse, up to what size?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the size limit is for the רבנן. It is setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even the רבנן cannot allow her to blame a huge stain on a louse, since a louse holds very little blood. So their view must also have some size limit, and the גמרא wants to know what it is.

phrases.english: And according to the Rabbis, who say she may blame a louse,
up to what size?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After giving רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's size limit, the גמרא asks for the limit according to the רבנן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The largest stain the רבנן allow her to blame on a creature.

steps.title: Bedbug, up to a lupine bean
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that according to the רבנן she may blame a bedbug, for a stain up to the size of a lupine bean.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: she may blame a bedbug, and up to the size of a lupine bean.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers the question from the last step. He explains how big a stain she may blame according to the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the רבנן, she may blame the stain on a פשפש (bedbug), and not only on a louse. Since a bedbug holds more blood, the limit is larger, up to the size of a lupine bean.
steps.whatToRemember: According to the רבנן, she may blame a stain on a bedbug, up to the size of a lupine bean.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
She may blame it on a bedbug,
and up to the size of a lupine bean.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: תּוֹלָה בְּפִשְׁפֵּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to the רבנן, she may blame a bedbug, for a stain up to the size of a lupine bean.

steps.title: A teaching describing the bedbug
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives three features of the פשפש: it is as long as it is wide, it tastes like it smells, and anyone who crushes it smells it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: This bedbug is as long as it is wide, and it tastes the way it smells. There is a fixed rule of nature about it: anyone who crushes it smells it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the topic of the פשפש from the last step by quoting a ברייתא that lists its features.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives three facts without saying why they matter. The next steps explain which הלכות each fact affects.

keyTerms.meaning: A covenant is made; a fixed rule of nature
One who crushes or squeezes it

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
This bedbug, its length is like its width,
and its taste is like its smell.
A covenant is made with it,
phrases.notes: He means it is a fixed law of nature that always happens.

phrases.english: that anyone who crushes it smells it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on the פשפש that רב נחמן בר יצחק just mentioned.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פשפש is square in shape, tastes like its smell, and always gives off a smell when crushed.

steps.title: Why the bedbug's shape matters: stains
steps.stepSummary: The fact that the bedbug is as long as it is wide matters for the laws of כתמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Its length is like its width' is said for the laws of stains.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the purpose of the first fact in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because a crushed bedbug leaves a stain as long as it is wide, a stain with that shape can be blamed on a bedbug. The shape itself becomes a sign of where the blood came from.

keyTerms.meaning: Blood stains found on a woman's body or clothing
With regard to; for the topic of

phrases.english: 'Its length is like its width' is for the matter of stains;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first feature listed in the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A stain shaped like a bedbug (as long as it is wide) may be blamed on a bedbug.

steps.title: Why the bedbug's taste matters: תרומה
steps.stepSummary: The fact that the bedbug tastes like it smells matters for תרומה, as a משנה says that someone eating תרומה who tastes a bedbug must spit it out.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Its taste is like its smell' is for the laws of תרומה. As we learned in a משנה: Or if he tasted the taste of a bedbug in his mouth, he must spit it out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second fact in the ברייתא and backs it up with a משנה about תרומה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally one may not waste תרומה. But if a person tastes a bedbug in his mouth, he must spit out the food so he does not swallow a forbidden bug.

keyTerms.meaning: The portion of produce given to a כהן, which may not be wasted

phrases.english: 'Its taste is like its smell' is for the matter of terumah.
As we learned in a Mishnah:
Or if he tasted the taste of a bedbug in his mouth,
he must spit it out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second feature of the ברייתא, the way step 26 explained the first.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who tastes a bedbug while eating תרומה must spit out the food.

steps.title: How does he know it is a bedbug?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the person eating תרומה can tell that he tasted a bedbug.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does he know?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question about the משנה: how can someone recognize a bedbug just by taste?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Spitting out תרומה is a serious step, so the person needs a reliable way to know it is a bedbug. The question sets up the use of the ברייתא's second fact.

phrases.english: How does he know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how the ruling of the משנה can be applied.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How a person can identify a bedbug in his mouth.

steps.title: Its taste is like its smell
steps.stepSummary: He knows because the bedbug tastes like it smells.
steps.simpleTranslation: Its taste is like its smell.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers using the ברייתא: the taste matches the bedbug's familiar smell.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he knows the smell, he can recognize the taste. This explains why the ברייתא bothered to say 'its taste is like its smell.'

keyTerms.meaning: Its taste is like its smell

phrases.english: Its taste is like its smell.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He recognizes the taste because it matches the bedbug's smell.

steps.title: But how does he know the smell?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes further: how does he know what a bedbug smells like?
steps.simpleTranslation: And still, how does he know?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is not satisfied yet and asks how a person would know the bedbug's smell in the first place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last answer depends on knowing the smell. So the question moves one level back: where does that knowledge come from?

phrases.english: And still, how does he know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the answer in step 29.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How a person knows what a bedbug smells like.

steps.title: Everyone who crushes one smells it
steps.stepSummary: He knows the smell because it is a fixed rule that anyone who crushes a bedbug smells it, so the smell is well known.
steps.simpleTranslation: A covenant is made with it: anyone who crushes it smells it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with the third fact of the ברייתא: everyone knows the smell from crushing bedbugs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since crushing a bedbug always releases its smell, people know it well. Now all three facts of the ברייתא have been explained.
steps.whatToRemember: Every fact in the ברייתא about the פשפש has a use: its shape helps with כתמים, and its taste and smell help someone eating תרומה know to spit it out.

phrases.english: A covenant is made with it,
that anyone who crushes it smells it.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּרִית כְּרוּתָה לוֹ, שֶׁכׇּל הַמּוֹלְלוֹ מֵרִיחַ בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 30 using the ברייתא of step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The smell is familiar to all, because crushing a bedbug always releases it.

steps.title: A town with pigs: no worry about stains
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי rules that in a town with pigs, stains are not a concern.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: In a town that has pigs, we are not concerned about stains.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a new rule about places where a stain can easily come from something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pigs carry blood and attract bugs, so a stain in such a town can always be blamed on them. This takes the idea of 'blaming' a stain to its widest form: the whole town gets the leniency.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
A town that has pigs in it,
we are not concerned about stains.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: עִיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ חֲזִירִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new point about blaming stains on outside sources.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a town with pigs, stains found on a woman do not make her impure.

steps.title: The town of דרוקרת counts as a pig town
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק adds that the town of דרוקרת is treated like a town with pigs.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: And this town of דרוקרת is like a town that has pigs.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק applies רב אשי's rule to a real town he knew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן בר יצחק compares דרוקרת to a town with pigs, so it gets the same leniency. The point is that a place full of outside sources of blood counts the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: Is similar to; is treated like

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
And this town of Droqeret
is like a town that has pigs in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: וְהָא דְּרוֹקֶרֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends רב אשי's rule to a specific place.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דרוקרת gets the same leniency as a town with pigs.

steps.title: רב הונא: a stain the size of a split bean may not be blamed
steps.stepSummary: Going back to the משנה's size limit, רב הונא says a stain the size of a גריס may not be blamed on a louse; only a smaller one may.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Up to how much may she blame,' etc. רב הונא said: If it is the size of a גריס, she may not blame it; less than a גריס, she may blame it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the line in the משנה about the size limit and starts to explain what 'up to a גריס' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'up to a גריס' are unclear: is the גריס itself included or not? רב הונא says it is not included, so only a stain smaller than a גריס may be blamed on a louse.

keyTerms.meaning: The size of a split bean
She blames it on something else (and stays pure)

phrases.english: 'Up to how much may she blame,' etc.
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting the משנה, where רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס said up to a split bean.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
The size of a split bean: she may not blame it,
less than a split bean: she may blame it,

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד כַּמָּה הִיא תּוֹלָה וְכוּ׳. אָמַר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה's size limit of רבי חנינא בן אנטיגנוס (steps 6 and 7) and starts explaining it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A stain exactly the size of a גריס may not be blamed on a louse; only smaller.

steps.title: רב חסדא: a split-bean stain may still be blamed
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא disagrees: a stain the size of a גריס may still be blamed; only a bigger one may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב חסדא said: The size of a גריס, she may blame it; more than a גריס, she may not blame it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives the opposite reading of 'up to a גריס.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב חסדא, the גריס itself is included in the leniency. The only stain that cannot be blamed on a louse is one bigger than a גריס.
steps.confusionAlert: Both agree that smaller than a גריס may be blamed and bigger than a גריס may not. They argue ONLY about a stain that is exactly the size of a גריס.
steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא: exactly a גריס may not be blamed. רב חסדא: exactly a גריס may still be blamed.

phrases.english: And Rav Ḥisda said:
The size of a split bean: she may blame it,
more than a split bean: she may not blame it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב הונא's reading of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A stain exactly the size of a גריס may still be blamed on a louse; only bigger may not.

steps.title: Do they argue about whether 'up to' includes the limit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רב הונא and רב חסדא argue about the general question of whether 'up to' includes the limit itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say they argue about 'up to and including'? רב הונא holds 'up to' does not include the limit, and רב חסדא holds it does include the limit?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers an idea: maybe the argument about a stain exactly the size of a גריס comes from a bigger, general question about how to read the word 'up to'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said a stain 'up to' a גריס may be blamed on a louse. If 'up to' leaves out the limit, a stain exactly a גריס is not covered, which is רב הונא's view. If 'up to' includes the limit, a stain exactly a גריס is covered, which is רב חסדא's view.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? It introduces a suggestion the גמרא will test
Up to and including the limit
Up to but not including the limit
A split bean, used as a size measure for stains

steps.confusionAlert: This is only a suggestion. The next two steps show that neither אמורא has to hold this way, so do not treat it as the final explanation.

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא, בְּעַד וְעַד בִּכְלָל קָא מִיפַּלְגִי,
phrases.english: Shall we say they argue about 'up to and including'?
phrases.notes: The משנה said a stain 'up to' a גריס can be blamed on a louse. Does that include a stain exactly a גריס?

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַב הוּנָא סָבַר: עַד וְלֹא עַד בִּכְלָל,
phrases.english: That Rav Huna holds: up to, but not including the limit,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב חִסְדָּא סָבַר: עַד וְעַד בִּכְלָל?
phrases.english: and Rav Chisda holds: up to and including the limit?

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא, בְּעַד וְעַד בִּכְלָל קָא מִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to explain the root of the argument in steps 34 and 35.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the argument between רב הונא and רב חסדא really a general argument about whether 'up to' includes the limit?

steps.title: רב הונא: 'up to' is always read the strict way
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא can say both readings exist, and each one is used where it gives the stricter result.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא can tell you: sometimes 'up to' includes the limit and sometimes it does not. Here the reading is strict, and there the reading is strict.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion from רב הונא's side. He does not hold that 'up to' never includes the limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא's rule is: pick whichever reading leads to the stricter result. With stains, leaving out the גריס itself is the strict reading, because then a stain exactly a גריס makes her טמאה. Somewhere else, including the limit might be the strict reading, and then he would include it.

keyTerms.meaning: For strictness, leading to the stricter result

phrases.english: Rav Huna can say to you:
There is 'up to and including the limit,'
and there is 'up to but not including the limit,'
and here it is for strictness, and there it is for strictness.
phrases.notes: He means each reading is chosen where it makes the law stricter. With stains, leaving out the גריס is the strict choice.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 36 as far as רב הונא is concerned.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that רב הונא holds 'up to' always leaves out the limit.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The suggestion assumed one fixed reading of 'up to'. In fact רב הונא picks the reading by which one is stricter.

steps.title: רב חסדא: stains are a lenient exception, following רבי אבהו
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא agrees that usually we read 'up to' strictly, but says stains are different because of רבי אבהו's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא can tell you: in general I agree we read it the strict way and not the lenient way. But here it follows רבי אבהו, who said: all measures of the חכמים are applied strictly, except the גריס of stains, which is applied leniently.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion from רב חסדא's side too. He agrees with רב הונא's general rule, but says stains are a special exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally רב חסדא would also choose the strict reading. But רבי אבהו taught that the גריס measure for stains is the one measure we apply leniently. So a stain exactly a גריס may still be blamed on a louse, and the woman stays טהורה.

keyTerms.meaning: For leniency, leading to the easier result
To be strict / to be lenient
Stains of blood found on a woman's clothing

steps.whatToRemember: Both אמוראים agree that 'up to' is usually read the strict way. They argue only about whether stains are an exception. רב חסדא says they are, based on רבי אבהו.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבי אבהו's rule, that the גריס of stains is the one measure we apply leniently, is a key source for being lenient with stains.

phrases.english: And Rav Chisda can say to you:
In general, I will tell you,
we say it for strictness; we do not say it for leniency.
But here it follows Rabbi Abbahu,
for Rabbi Abbahu said:
All measures of the Sages are applied strictly,
except for the split-bean size of stains, which is applied leniently.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes rejecting step 36 by showing רב חסדא also does not depend on it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that רב חסדא holds 'up to' always includes the limit.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב חסדא agrees with the general strict rule. His lenient view comes only from the special rule of רבי אבהו about stains.

steps.title: A second version: the argument stated on its own
steps.stepSummary: Some present the argument as a separate teaching. רב הונא treats a גריס like more than a גריס, and רב חסדא treats it like less, and they argue about 'up to' in this case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some teach this argument as a teaching on its own. רב הונא says: a stain the size of a גריס is like one bigger than a גריס. רב חסדא says: a stain the size of a גריס is like one smaller than a גריס. They argue about the 'up to' here, as we explained. A challenge was raised:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different version of the argument, not tied to explaining the משנה, but argued directly about this case. Then it starts a challenge, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the argument is only about the 'up to' in the case of stains. רב הונא counts a גריס-sized stain with the bigger stains, so it is not blamed on a louse. רב חסדא counts it with the smaller stains, so it is. The word מיתיבי at the end opens a challenge from a teaching of the תנאים, which appears on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: On its own, as a separate teaching

phrases.aramaic: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי לַהּ לְהָא שְׁמַעְתָּא בְּאַפֵּי נַפְשַׁהּ:
phrases.english: Some say this teaching as a separate matter:

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא אָמַר — כִּגְרִיס כְּיָתֵר מִכִּגְרִיס,
phrases.english: Rav Huna says: the size of a split bean is like more than a split bean,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר — כִּגְרִיס כְּפָחוֹת מִכִּגְרִיס,
phrases.english: and Rav Chisda says: the size of a split bean is like less than a split bean,
and they argue about the 'up to' here, as we said.
They raised an objection:

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי לַהּ לְהָא שְׁמַעְתָּא בְּאַפֵּי נַפְשַׁהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of the argument in steps 34 and 35, then begins a challenge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא: a גריס-sized stain counts as more than a גריס. רב חסדא: it counts as less than a גריס. They argue about the 'up to' of this case.
